Different ways of existing do not necessarily mean different natures. The same kind may exist materially and immaterially, or the same thing may have these modes at different times or in different respects.

The commentator says the issue is simple: features considered universally differ from features considered as particular, sensed things. The author’s answer also treats existence as a feature, and the ways in which a nature exists can differ.
The wording is loose. The point may be that knowing a material thing means knowing an imaginal or intellectual form of it.
This answer depends on the second and third premises of the proof.

The form of the argument is this: a bodily power cannot act without the body, but the intellect is said to contain the form without the body. If the original premise is true, its reversal is true too.

Here “being present” means being joined with or paired with something. If the form is joined to the intellect, it is also joined to the intellect’s subject. Otherwise, the same form would exist in two subjects at once.

The objection assumes that the soul must always attend to every feature it has. But it may have a feature without thinking about it. Its knowledge is present while it is actively aware; when attention turns away, that knowledge is no longer present as an act. The same is true of bodily feelings such as anger or fear.

Someone may ask why sleep, which leaves the outer senses and movement quiet, does not always make understanding stronger. The reply is that inner senses and natural powers become more active in sleep, and imagination occupies the soul. While awake, the outer senses can correct imagination; in sleep, they cannot, so imagination and estimation gain influence over the intellect.

The claim is only that the soul acts without the body in some activities, such as the three listed here. This avoids the common claim that the soul depends on matter for its acts even though it exists without matter.

Understanding is usually described as being affected, not acting. The reply is that “action” is used broadly here for any operation. Direct self-awareness is not an added act separate from the self; it is the self’s own presence to itself. The argument reaches its conclusion by considering the idea of self-awareness, not by assuming that the self and its awareness are two separate things.

One may object that knowing that one knows is itself acquired knowledge, and therefore not always present. If it were present without any intermediary, it should always remain. The first claim about direct self-awareness also does not count as an added act, since it is identical with the self.
This note supports the broad use of “action” in the argument, including being acted upon.

If a quality depends on a subject for its existence, saying that it can act without the subject only strengthens the claim that it needs the subject. How could something exist independently of what it necessarily depends on?

If the opponent means that powers act independently within their subjects, that claim can be accepted only if the powers themselves are immaterial. The author’s own view is that a body also contributes to the effect, because the relation and position needed for an effect require a body. The body’s role is not independent, but it is still real. The opposing account would leave bodily powers with no work to do.

Some copies may have reversed the wording of the earlier claim about whether a power can act weakly after acting strongly, or strongly after acting weakly. The author’s reasoning and examples do not make the intended direction entirely clear. Practice may also matter: a power that has become used to a weak act may not manage a strong one.
The point is that a power suited to strong action cannot simply perform a weak action, and a weak power cannot simply perform a strong one. Each act requires a matching power.
The idea is that the intellect does not tire after many acts, unlike bodily powers. This appears to be the intended reading of the author’s argument.

Someone might deny that the strength of an imagined form matches the strength of the thing as it exists outside the mind. Even if so, mental images can still be stronger or weaker than one another. The mind can move from a powerful image to a weaker one without losing its ability to perceive. What matters is that imagination is not limited in the way bodily powers are. Becoming absorbed in an image is also different from being unable to imagine a weaker thing at all.
It is the imagined thing, not the act of imagining, that the opponent calls “small.”

The soul’s unity, and the intellect’s unity if it is immaterial, are unified in a way that gathers many powers into one. A body and powers imprinted in it have only numerical unity. Even if bodily powers can act, they cannot act in the immaterial way attributed to intellect; bodily action depends on position and relation, which cannot apply to nonexistent things. If several distinct powers were bodily, each would need its own subject, but the argument assumes only one body.
This point does not answer the objection; it is a separate argument.
The second case occurs when a cause remains but something blocks its effect. Once the obstacle is removed, the cause can act again.

An idea might return because a new inner cause replaces the original outside cause. The argument works only if the returning idea is numerically the same as the one that was forgotten. On that reading, it is really a further argument about memory.
Many copies say “ten arguments,” but the correct reading is “eleven arguments.”

Depending on reports alone is not enough; reports joined with reason are a light added to light. Reports can also awaken the intellect before it has reached this understanding. Souls with strong intellectual support are rare.
The verse about breathing God’s spirit applies to Adam and to human beings generally. Other verses describe the creation of the human being from clay and the command that the angels bow to Adam.

If “My spirit” is an honorific relation, the verse points to the spirit’s immaterial nature, since a created effect resembles its source. If the wording means that the spirit is distinct from God, it points to a still higher state, beyond matter and perhaps even beyond essence as ordinarily understood. The same applies to “His Word”: divine speech is immaterial, unlike bodily speech or an imagined voice.
The spirit’s relation to God is not just a way of describing it; God brings it into existence directly.
The one who perceives and what is perceived must have something in common. The body cannot perceive the immaterial kingdom of heaven.
The verse emphasizes the human being’s new creation, then praises God as the best creator.

The reference to pairs may include the body and soul of the next life, existence and essence, and God’s face and the soul’s face. “What they do not know” may include the unseen worlds and the “good word,” which the Imams sometimes use of themselves. True unity means that the human being becomes a state of being and returns to God by taking on divine qualities.

If the soul were imprinted in the body, then at death it would either perish with its subject, or move to another body. The first would rule out the soul’s survival; the second would require an accident or bodily power to move from one subject to another.

“Whoever knows himself knows his Lord” has several meanings. A person may see the soul as a meeting point of dependence and independence, or as a mirror for all divine names. The soul can also serve as a small-scale example of God’s being, qualities, and acts: it is not confined to a place, knows itself, acts by intention, and has a kind of power and love. Or a person may recognize that they own nothing and that every act belongs to God. Knowing that the self changes and comes to be also points to God as the lasting source of existence; knowing its weakness points to divine power. In each case, knowledge of the self leads to knowledge of God.

The Prophet’s private “time with God” is a state in which the limits that distinguish one being from another fall away. Gabriel said that coming any closer would burn him. The report does not mean a meeting in physical space.

“How You give life to the dead” may also refer to seeing how God gives life: consider bodies on their own, then see the souls and intellects that give them life as belonging to the divine realm. In that sense, bodies are dead in themselves. When viewed through the divine source, they are immaterial. A similar interpretation appears in Rumi’s Masnavi.
The two fingers may also mean God’s gentleness and severity, fear and hope, or contraction and expansion.

The spirits’ priority to bodies is essential or timeless, not a period of two thousand ordinary years. The numbers refer symbolically to the realms of soul and intellect, each of which displays a thousand divine names.

The phrase that Imam ‘Ali was “possessed by God” means he was overwhelmed by nearness to God, like the hadith in which God becomes the hearing and sight of the servant who draws near to Him. This explains how he could perform extraordinary acts through divine power.

The number seventy thousand may describe the soul’s many levels—soul, heart, intellect, spirit, secret, hidden, and most hidden—with ten powers at each level. It may also refer to the many powers and kinds of nature present in the soul. In either case, the number expresses abundance: the human spirit contains the powers found throughout the world.

Aristotle’s statement “without a body” avoids suggesting that the soul returns to a body through reincarnation. The author reads it as a description of spiritual ascent. Two points matter: a person is not identical with the visible body, and knowledge of God, the divine qualities and acts, and the next life must be sought for its own sake—not as a tool for worldly gain. Otherwise, the soul remains earthbound. Few people actually reach that destination.
The meaning of the soul’s “fault,” “fall,” and escape from this world will be discussed later, in the section on how the soul comes to be.

Souls differ in whether they are intellect only in potential or intellect in reality. The same soul can also differ over time: it begins with a bodily origin and may end as spiritual. Even at one time, it can act like an animal while absorbed in bodily life, and like an angel while absorbed in God or in knowledge of the first and last things.
The two wings are theoretical reason and practical reason.
If it is not necessary for the world to lack intellect, then it is possible for it to have one. In the realm of creation, a thing’s possibility is enough for it to be brought into being.

The argument also relies on the principle that a higher kind of existence cannot arise directly from a purely lower one. Here “intellect” can mean the source of a kind, while the soul of a simple element or compound may be its imaginal form. Intellectual forms are the intellectual life of a thing; its imaginal forms are its life and knowledge in the world of images. “Then He sent our souls” may repeat the general point for emphasis, or refer specifically to the souls of the heavenly spheres.
Some religious scholars, like the philosophers, used reasoning to discuss the spirit.

“The Throne” may mean the outermost sphere, with “what it contains” referring to the world of images. It may also mean the all-embracing existence or universal mercy, with everything limited contained within it. In that reading, the saying describes the soul’s absorption in God.

The statement that spirit is present in dense matter seems to make it a bodily quality. It can be understood instead to mean that the spirit gives life to things. The phrase “spirit is a name” may mean that the name is known while the spirit’s true nature is not. The living source present in things is the meaning behind the name. The wording is difficult, but it need not imply that the spirit is an accident in a body.
If the spirit is God’s word, then it exists in God, not in a physical body.

Scholars’ disagreement may come from how they read the word “from” in “the spirit is from the command of my Lord.” If it means “coming from,” the spirit was created. If it means “belonging to,” it may be eternal with God’s command. This resembles the debate over whether God’s speech is eternal or created, and a similar debate appears among philosophers.

“Made in their form” may mean that spirits have inward organs matching the human form, or that their outward form is human. In either case, the spirits are not bodily. The angels may be the sources of kinds, or the angels who govern rain and other natural events.

The “spirit” may mean Gabriel, with whom the human rational soul becomes united after changes and growth in its very being. On that reading, what is said of Gabriel also helps explain the perfected human soul. The Throne is greater than this spirit because it stands for all-embracing mercy and the divine gift of existence. Gabriel is one of the bearers of the Throne.

The statement that the spirit could swallow the heavens means that the heavens are like a ring in a vast open country compared with the world of intellect. Gabriel also has a true form, in which the Prophet is said to have seen him twice, filling the two horizons, and an appearance suited to the human beings who see him—such as the form of Diḥya al-Kalbī in the Prophet's time.

Gabriel is said to stand on the right of the Throne because the right stands for the stronger side, and immaterial beings belong to higher levels of existence. On this symbolic map, the holy intellects occupy the upper right, universal souls the lower right, independent imaginal forms the upper left, and universal natures the lower left. Gabriel's intercession for those who affirm God's oneness means bringing them from what they are capable of becoming to what they actually achieve. What is now an inward change will appear as intercession in the life to come.

There is another possible reading. The spirit may be the human spirit itself, and the greater Throne may mean the full order of divine knowledge or the heart of a perfected human being, which is called God's Throne. The statement then resembles praise expressed in a form that sounds like a qualification. The perfected soul contains the higher heavens within its own existence, to say nothing of their imaginal and physical counterparts. As a Persian verse puts it, there are heavens within the realm of the soul that govern the heavens of this world.

Another poet pictures a bird that takes in thorns with the whole rose garden and finds what is bitter sweet. The point is that the perfected soul can contain the signs of divine gentleness and divine power together. Its “form” is not merely an outward shape: it is what makes it fully what it is. Its “face” may indicate the imaginal appearance closest to its true being, a form corresponding to the human form. Its place on the right has the same symbolic meaning as before.

The soul also intercedes by displaying a reflected form of divine unity. It gathers qualities that point to God's transcendence and qualities that point to His presence in creation, making the truth of oneness easier for others to understand. Its light burns with such force that ordinary bodily appearance veils it. As another line suggests, the sun appears in human form with its face covered. God knows best.

The speaker may mean that the spirit belongs to the world of command, not the natural world of things that come to be and pass away. “Be” can also mean existence itself, spread through spirits and bodies. The highest spirits do not need a separate command to exist; they are themselves a command and pure existence.

This refers to the spirits’ affirmation of God in the primordial covenant. The author explains it through several levels of existence, from the divine names and intellects down to the soul and world of images. At each level, existence belongs to God; created natures have only a dependent existence, like images that depend on a mirror. In this world, matter and time make things seem separate and self-sufficient, but some remain faithful to the covenant and know that all existence belongs to God.
“Hidden things” includes not only what is imagined, but also what is estimated and what is understood. All are hidden in relation to the senses.

Reports that spirits visit their homes on Friday nights can be explained by saying that the barriers to perception are lifted, while the soul’s powers of awareness remain. The worlds of this life and the next are therefore alike to the spirit. A soul that has reached a high divine station, however, longs for the life of union with luminous intellects and does not turn back toward lesser images. “The angels speak in heaven” should be read as something the spirits see. “Spirits beneath the Throne” means spirits from the higher realm. In “an intermediate place on earth,” the word “from” marks where the journey begins.

This means the sins for which people are punished while still alive. The wording suggests that the dead receive a reason to ask that the living be forgiven. A hardship that afflicts everyone can make an excuse for each person; the passage hints at a well-known saying by the poet ‘Umar Khayyam.
“They have fallen” means “they have fallen into the abyss.”
“The Hour” here means the great Resurrection and the final unveiling. A person’s death is also a resurrection, but on a smaller or intermediate scale.

If the world of images exists, descriptions of spirits with forms do not conflict with immateriality. They strengthen the point, because the spirit can exist in both an imaginal and an intellectual mode.

The claim that humanity and animal life are created in a person can refer to the natural, bodily human and animal forms, which death removes. Or it can refer to human and animal life across all worlds, which only complete spiritual passing away removes. At a deeper level, existence is the true reality of a person, while what we call the person’s essence is a feature drawn from a particular level of existence.

“Spirit” may mean the body’s vital spirit, which is interwoven with the body. Likewise, saying the soul is a subtle body flowing through the body like water through a flower or fire through coal may refer to the soul’s lowest level.

Ibn ‘Abbas was a respected student of Imam ‘Ali. His words might seem to say that spirits perish when bodies perish, just as a lamp’s light disappears when its oil is gone. The author says he meant the opposite: when a branch lamp goes out, its light returns to the lasting source from which it came. So souls, especially those perfected in life, return to the Holy Spirit or active intellect when their bodies decay. The comparison with flesh in sickness also suggests that the body’s true form can remain in the next life even when its material parts have changed.
These movements of thought may be intellectual or practical.

This answers the claim that the afterlife is only spiritual and cannot include particular bodily pleasures or pains. The author says the soul has particular, immaterial powers of perception of its own. These are subtler than intellect, but survive with the soul. That is why al-Ghazali says the soul carries its power of estimation after death.
“The spirit” here is the rational soul in its immaterial state; “animal spirit” is the soul’s capacity for sense and movement; its bodily home is the vital spirit, which carries these powers.

When the spirit from the world of command enters the animal spirit, the animal spirit becomes a new kind of thing. The animal spirit may be treated as a broad kind, while the human spirit gives it its essential distinguishing feature.
This follows the idea of a marriage that continues through all generations.

The lamp is the light of God's oneness. The comparison with the heart's tapering shape is fitting. The heart of a believer who understands is a world of intellect that mirrors the world outside. We can picture the order of existence as a cone of light: its narrow point is towards God, and its broad base towards matter. Nearer God, oneness and simplicity are clearer; nearer matter, multiplicity and composition increase.

In the report, the unbeliever's heart is described as dark because the world is, for that person, like a cone of darkness. It is turned upside down because attention rests on the many things of the bodily world without turning towards the unity that gathers them, and on outward forms without reaching their deeper meaning.

A commentator distinguishes several kinds of unbelief. Some people have not received the prophetic message, or have not understood parts of it. He calls this unbelief through ignorance and says that many of these people, because of their limited opportunity, may not be punished. Others hear the message but reject it through pride, inherited loyalties, or prejudice: this is deliberate rejection. Still others affirm the message outwardly, perhaps to protect their lives or property, while denying it inwardly: this is hypocrisy, which the commentator regards as more serious.

A further case is someone who privately accepts the truth but refuses to admit it, out of envy, stubbornness, or deference to others. The commentator treats this as a different kind of concealment. Another person may affirm the message in speech and belief yet misunderstand it because of poor judgment or misleading teachers. This is error, and its seriousness varies with the extent of the error.

Lastly, a person may understand and accept the message yet disobey its commands while recognising the wrong. Some texts also use “unbelief” for this kind of wrongdoing. The commentator notes that other schools disagree over whether a grave sinner should be called an unbeliever, a believer, or neither. He does not treat every case as deserving the same judgment or punishment.

The image of the dark, inverted heart can cover these different cases. Hypocrisy receives a separate image—the heart bound as if to a stake—because the person keeps the inner denial concealed while presenting the opposite outwardly. Someone who knows the truth but rejects it openly is different in that respect. The report's heart with two faces corresponds to the self that reproaches itself, pulled between contrary tendencies. — س ره

The author has described four of the human being’s seven levels: soul, heart, intellect, and spirit. He leaves the final three—the secret, the hidden, and the most hidden—without explanation, since they are known through direct experience.
Some manuscript copies read “the body is understood” rather than “the body is an intellect.”

This kind of dependence is strongest because a thing’s nature and its existence depend on each other in meaning, both in the mind and in reality. The relation is present even in thought; it is not merely that we choose to consider one thing alongside another. Every nature that exists requires existence, though existence can also be without a nature, as in separate intellects. A thing with an essence therefore depends in two ways: in its essence and in its existence.

The example is the existence of a possible thing depending on the Necessary Being. One may also read this as the possibility or neediness of the possible thing itself, without supplying the word “existence.”

An image needs matter in order to be an individual image, but not to be the kind of image it is. By contrast, a quality such as blackness depends both for its individual presence and its kind of existence on a particular subject. The subject must be an actual individual, not just some possible subject in general.

This type of dependence lasts only as long as the thing exists, not in its nature as such. It differs from the third kind, which lasts from the thing’s coming to be through its continued existence, and from the fifth, where the dependence is needed only at the beginning. The list may not cover every kind of relation: for example, two related things may each depend on the other in meaning.

The fifth kind depends on the nature of the thing it relies on, as the soul depends on bodily matter at the beginning. The body is the soul’s matter, so the soul’s need is general rather than for one particular body.

The soul depends on the body for completion only after it has gained its bodily form and practical powers, and before its theoretical intellect becomes actual. Once it has reached intellectual completion, it no longer depends on the body in this way; it can seem to put the body off like a garment.
If the soul had to use sight in order to perceive what is seen, and hearing for what is heard, then the soul would not be one simple perceiver.
Losing a sense may mean losing knowledge of the sensible things that belong to it, or losing the general understanding drawn from those particular things.

On the usual account, the intellect abstracts general ideas from particular things and makes those forms. On the author’s account, the soul understands universals by witnessing their sources in the world of intellect, and the knower becomes one with what is known. “Making” an idea can then mean that the soul itself becomes an intellect, or that the universals are titles and reflections of those higher sources.

The claim that the soul has only one level means, on the opposing view, that it remains numerically the same with no inward movement or change in its very existence. The author also holds that one soul has many levels, but for him these are stages of one developing being. The soul can show the qualities of the natural world, even of basic matter, and can also take on the qualities associated with God. Between those extremes lie many stages.

The Qur'anic verse speaks of a time that passed “over the human being.” This wording suggests that even the stage of bare matter, and not only the stages of plant or animal life, can belong to the history of a human soul. That is not surprising if we mean matter and nature as stages along a person's own path of development. It would be surprising if we meant a plant, animal, or piece of matter standing outside that path, with no such movement. Considered in themselves, those separate things are not stages of this human being.

The author gives one possible meaning of the verse. A higher reading is that it refers to the human being's prior existence in the divine realm. There, the fixed reality of a human being belonged to the level of God's names and attributes and was known directly through His knowledge. The “time” mentioned in the verse is like the “time” in the Prophet's saying, “I have a time with God.” It does not mean an ordinary period measured by clocks. The person did not yet exist through a separate existence of their own. Rather, all these realities were present through God's existence. There was not yet the scattered multitude of limited, material beings we see here.

Even in the lower worlds, light prevails over darkness, mercy comes before anger, and unity has precedence over multiplicity. But those signs are far from the undivided reality of that earlier divine level.
The distinction between these two kinds of form follows from eight differences discussed earlier, in the section on intellect and intelligible forms.

Views on the soul’s beginning can be sorted into two broad camps. Those who say it comes to be disagree about whether it existed before the body, began with the body, or was created through the body so that the body’s coming to be is also its own. Those who say it is eternal may mean that it is eternal by nature, as in the extreme view that the soul is God; eternal in time but created in its nature; eternal among many bodies, as those who believe in souls moving between bodies say; or eternal in a higher chain of existence as a universal intellect. The last view is Plato’s.

The heavens were thought by some philosophers to be eternal, though subject to weakness as their positions change; Sadra also says their substance changes. The point is: even if the soul were eternal, its immaterial nature would make it complete and free of weakness.

One could object that species reproduced over generations are eternal and have many individuals. The reply is that what matters is not eternity but being free of changing accidents that create many individuals. The kind survives by one individual following another; it is not one eternal individual.

The point is that this is not a feature found in every case. We should not object that the celestial bodies, too, each have a kind limited to one individual: having only one individual is not a feature reserved for immaterial beings.

There is another answer, one that follows the author's philosophy and that of the leading sages. The heavenly spheres and the kinds of things that reproduce are coming into being and passing away in their very substance. Their existence changes at every moment. What looks like one lasting individual is, in reality, a continuous succession of stages, each coming after the disappearance of what preceded it and passing away before what follows.
